title: Vidorama - technical deep dive: Dedicated shapes + benchmark methodology
topics: Workload overview (high QPS, mixed context lengths, streaming)
Hardware shapes by region (H100 vs A100 vs L40S)
Benchmark methodology (tokens/sec attribution, warmup, batch/ctx controls)
Operational considerations (autoscaling, queueing, admission control, observability)
summary: Vidorama walked Redwood through a high-QPS generation workload (primarily chat-style, streaming, short prompts with occasional long-context requests). Redwood Infra and Solutions explained the current Dedicated shape catalog (H100/A100/L40S families), how Redwood runs benchmarks (steady-state, warmed, fixed model version, controlled batching and context distributions), and why tokens/sec varies across model architecture and sequence length. The group aligned on a proposed initial shape for a US-East deployment, plus a plan to run a short benchmark using Vidorama’s prompt/response distributions to validate throughput floors and tail latency before finalizing tier + commit size.
questions: How does Redwood measure tokens/sec for streaming responses (do partial tokens count, what about client disconnects)?
How much variance should we expect between short-context and long-context traffic on the same pool?
What headroom does Redwood assume for a Dedicated commitment (especially for bursty traffic)?
Can we pin a model version and still get predictable throughput if you roll kernels/runtime updates?
If we start on A100, how hard is it to migrate to H100 later without re-integration?
action_items: Redwood (Simran): send Vidorama the benchmark input template (prompt set format + traffic mix fields) and the run instructions by 2025-03-05.
Vidorama (Priya/Jason): provide 24h traffic histogram (RPS/QPS, input/output token percentiles, streaming vs non-streaming split) by 2025-03-07.
Redwood (Irene/Nina): propose 2 candidate Dedicated shapes in us-east and eu-west with expected steady-state tokens/sec ranges for Vidorama’s model shortlist by 2025-03-08.
Redwood (Markus): schedule a 30-min follow-up to review benchmark results and sizing recommendation by 2025-03-11.
next_steps: Share Vidorama traffic mix + prompt set
Redwood runs a controlled benchmark on 1–2 candidate shapes in the target region(s)
Review results (throughput/latency) and pick initial Dedicated shape + scaling policy
Confirm model/version pinning and any long-context constraints before commercial proposal

Fireflies.ai transcript

Title: Vidorama - technical deep dive: Dedicated shapes + benchmark methodology
Date: 2025-03-03
Time: 17:00 UTC
Duration: 57 minutes

Attendees (Redwood): Markus Klein, Simran Kaur, Irene Choi, Nina Petrova
Attendees (Vidorama): Miguel Santos (CTO), Priya Desai (ML Engineer), Jason Wu (Platform Eng), Evan Brooks (ML Ops)

---

[00:00] Markus Klein: Cool. Alright, thanks everyone for making time. This is the deep dive on shapes and benchmarks. We’ll try to keep it practical: what shape options, what we can actually guarantee, how we measure, and how we’d size for your QPS.

[00:14] Miguel Santos: Sounds good.

[00:16] Markus Klein: Priya, Jason, if you wanna do a quick recap of the workload just so Irene and Nina have it fresh.

[00:23] Priya Desai: Yeah. So we have… um, video summarization and also like conversational search over clips. The user experience is chat-like, mostly streaming. We’re at peak like 1.8 to 2.2k QPS on weekdays. It’s spiky because of notifications.

[00:42] Priya Desai: Prompt sizes are small-ish usually, like 150 to 400 input tokens. Output maybe 80 to 250. But we have a long context mode where we attach a transcript chunk, which can be like 8k or 12k input tokens. That’s maybe 6% of traffic.

[01:02] Jason Wu: And we care about p95 latency. It’s not just average. We can tolerate a bit of queueing, but not seconds.

[01:11] Markus Klein: Got it. And model wise you said you’re evaluating open models plus you currently call—sorry I’ll say it—Azure OpenAI sometimes for the long context, right?

[01:20] Miguel Santos: Yeah, we do. It’s expensive. We’d rather bring more of it to a dedicated pool.

[01:27] Markus Klein: Makes sense. Simran, you wanna frame how we think about “shape” and what the benchmark outputs actually mean?

[01:33] Simran Kaur: Sure. So in Redwood Dedicated, you’re basically buying a reserved GPU pool. We standardize that into a handful of hardware shapes per region—like “8x H100” or “8x A100” variants, and in some regions “8x L40S” for cost sensitivity.

[01:50] Simran Kaur: The tricky thing is tokens/sec depends on model architecture, quantization profile, sequence length distribution, and whether you’re streaming. So our benchmarks are always tied to: model + version, a known serving config, and an input/output distribution.

[02:04] Jason Wu: When you say tokens/sec, is it per user request? Or for the whole pool?

[02:09] Simran Kaur: Whole pool, aggregated. We can also show per-route, but the guarantee we’re working toward is per Dedicated deployment. Nina can talk about the metric semantics but the short version is: we measure produced tokens at the server side, divided by wall time, in a window.

[02:26] Nina Petrova: Yeah, and important: it’s “delivered tokens” not “requested.” Like if the client disconnects mid-stream, we stop counting after the disconnect, because the work stops. There’s some edge cases there and we’ve been fixing double-counting in streaming paths.

[02:41] Priya Desai: That was actually one of my questions. Like, if a user cancels, do we get weird inflation or deflation?

[02:46] Nina Petrova: Historically, some systems double-count streaming chunks. We had a bug in a different path where chunk boundaries were counted twice, but that’s fixed in the current runtime. For SLO reporting, we use the canonical “generated_token_total” counter from the inference engine, not the SDK.

[03:04] Irene Choi: Also, if you do aggressive client retries, you can make tokens/sec look “bad” because you’re effectively wasting compute. We treat that as a customer-side pattern, not a platform miss. We’ll still help debug, but it’s not something we’d credit against a throughput commitment.

[03:19] Miguel Santos: Understood. Let’s get into the shapes. We’re currently in us-east primarily. EU later.

[03:27] Irene Choi: Okay. For us-east, the standard shapes we have available right now are:
- 8x H100 80GB (NVLink) with a pretty beefy CPU/RAM pairing.
- 8x A100 80GB (NVLink) as a more available option.
- And 8x L40S 48GB in a couple zones, but that has different perf characteristics.

[03:48] Irene Choi: We also have some 4x variants but for your QPS, you’ll probably want at least an 8x pool for stable tail latency and to avoid running at 90%+ all the time.

[03:58] Jason Wu: What’s the networking and storage like? We had issues with some providers where EBS throughput or whatever becomes the limiter.

[04:06] Irene Choi: For Dedicated pools we use local NVMe for model weights and KV spill when applicable, and we design so you’re not bottlenecked on network for the intra-node GPU comms. The important factor for you is whether your workload is “single node” or “multi node” sharded. For many models, 8 GPUs is within one node, so you avoid cross-node latency.

[04:28] Nina Petrova: Yeah, and when it does go multi-node, we’re explicit: there’s a different shape and we’ll show you the perf delta. But for the model sizes you’ve mentioned—like 7B to 70B—an 8x single box is typical.

[04:43] Priya Desai: So H100 vs A100—what’s the real world tokens/sec? I know you can’t promise a number without our distribution, but like… order of magnitude?

[04:54] Simran Kaur: For a “chatty” distribution—short prompts, modest outputs—H100 can be 1.5x to 2.5x A100, but it depends. For longer context, the gap can change because memory bandwidth and attention kernels behave differently.

[05:10] Nina Petrova: And if you’re doing 8k to 12k input tokens, the prompt processing stage dominates. That tends to hit a different part of the stack than steady decode. So you’ll see tokens/sec drop as context length goes up.

[05:26] Jason Wu: That’s what worries us. The long-context traffic is low percentage but it can mess up the pool.

[05:31] Markus Klein: Yeah, exactly. This is why we often recommend either a separate route/pool for long context or at least separate concurrency controls, so the tail doesn’t blow up the core chat traffic.

[05:44] Miguel Santos: We’d like to avoid managing two pools if possible.

[05:48] Markus Klein: We can start with one and see, but we’ll probably advise some isolation once you have a few thousand QPS. Nina, can you explain how batching interacts with mixed traffic?

[05:58] Nina Petrova: Sure. The runtime does continuous batching. It’s great for throughput at high QPS, but the batch composition matters. If you mix short and very long prompts in the same batch, the long ones can hold the batch “open” longer, which can increase latency for the short ones.

[06:14] Nina Petrova: So we typically set max_batch_tokens and some queueing limits. For a mixed distribution, we may use separate queue lanes or route long-context requests to a different queue with a lower concurrency cap.

[06:28] Priya Desai: Is that something we configure? Or you do it?

[06:31] Nina Petrova: We expose it as config, but for Dedicated we usually own the defaults and tune with you. You can request a different profile, but we’ll validate it.

[06:41] Jason Wu: Can we just set a “max context” and reject anything above, say, 8k?

[06:46] Simran Kaur: Yes, and that’s actually commonly part of the Dedicated contract language: supported max context per model and per shape. If you send bigger than supported, we’ll return an error rather than degrade.

[07:00] Miguel Santos: Ok. Benchmarks—how do you run them? Like, are these synthetic? Or do you replay our prompts?

[07:07] Simran Kaur: Ideally you give us a representative prompt set and a distribution: input tokens P50/P95/P99, output tokens, and streaming ratio. Then we run controlled load against a pinned model version in a warmed environment.

[07:23] Simran Kaur: “Warmed” means the model weights are already loaded, KV cache is in steady state, and we exclude the initial cold start. We run for long enough to get stable p95/p99—usually 20 to 40 minutes.

[07:38] Evan Brooks: Do you simulate our clients? We have mobile clients, plus a server-side aggregator.

[07:44] Nina Petrova: We don’t need to simulate mobile. We just need the request pattern: concurrency, inter-arrival times, token lengths. The client matters mostly for cancellations/retries. If you have weird retry behavior, it can distort results.

[08:00] Jason Wu: We do have timeouts at 12 seconds and then we retry once.

[08:05] Nina Petrova: That’s fine; we just want to incorporate it or disable it for benchmarking so it doesn’t create feedback loops.

[08:13] Miguel Santos: How do you report the results? Like tokens/sec, latency, what else?

[08:19] Simran Kaur: We’ll give you: total output tokens/sec, request throughput, p50/p95/p99 time-to-first-token for streaming, plus end-to-end completion times. We also provide GPU utilization and queue time metrics.

[08:35] Markus Klein: And we’ll talk in ranges rather than a single number, because there’s variance.

[08:41] Priya Desai: Variance due to what? Just noisy neighbors?

[08:44] Irene Choi: Dedicated means no noisy neighbors on your GPUs. Variance is more about the workload distribution changing and sometimes kernel selection differences with sequence length. Also if you change the model version or quantization profile, it changes.

[09:00] Priya Desai: So if we pin a model version, do you still roll runtime updates under us?

[09:06] Markus Klein: We do, but we can coordinate. The intent is: model version is pinned, and runtime updates are backward compatible. If there’s a performance regression risk, we do canary, and for Dedicated we can delay.

[09:20] Nina Petrova: Also we keep a “known good” kernel set for common models. If an update shifts performance, we can roll back. Observability dashboards will show a step change.

[09:33] Jason Wu: Ok. Let’s talk sizing. We have 2k QPS peak. If avg output is 150 tokens, that’s 300k tokens/sec output. That seems… huge.

[09:44] Simran Kaur: Right, but careful: 2k QPS with 150 output tokens each is 300k output tokens/sec if they all complete in one second, which they don’t. It’s more like concurrent requests. We need concurrency and average duration.

[10:01] Jason Wu: Fair. Our average completion is like 2 to 3 seconds for a typical response. TTFT target under 700ms p95.

[10:11] Nina Petrova: That’s useful. Your “in-flight” could be 4k to 6k concurrent at peak if you have 2–3 seconds end-to-end, depending on streaming.

[10:23] Miguel Santos: Which is why we need predictable queueing.

[10:26] Markus Klein: Exactly. For Dedicated, the approach is: pick a shape and then set a utilization target, like 60–70% steady, so bursts don’t push you into saturation.

[10:39] Irene Choi: From fleet perspective, we typically plan headroom. For high-QPS customers, we recommend sizing so that your p95 stays within bounds even with batch size variance.

[10:52] Priya Desai: Can you give a concrete example? Like what an 8x H100 can do on a 70B class model?

[11:01] Nina Petrova: With the caveat: it depends on model and context. For a 70B-ish dense model, short prompts, moderate decode, an 8x H100 can sustain tens of thousands of output tokens per second. But when you push 8k+ prompts, it drops significantly.

[11:18] Priya Desai: That’s still not close to 300k.

[11:21] Simran Kaur: Right, which is why the earlier back-of-napkin was not the right mapping. We need your real concurrency and average tokens.

[11:29] Jason Wu: We can pull a histogram. We have p50 input 220 tokens, p95 input 900, p99 like 6k because of that long mode. Output p50 120, p95 280.

[11:44] Simran Kaur: Perfect. If you can send those plus a rate curve by hour, we can model it.

[11:52] Evan Brooks: How do you treat caching? We have system prompts that are common across requests.

[11:58] Nina Petrova: Prefix caching can help a lot. If your system prompt is identical, we can cache the KV for it. But it depends: are you changing the system prompt frequently? Is it per-user?

[12:10] Priya Desai: It’s mostly static. We add a few flags.

[12:13] Nina Petrova: Great. That can reduce prompt compute significantly, especially for the short prompt majority. But for the long-context transcript attachments, caching is less effective.

[12:27] Jason Wu: If caching is on, does that affect the throughput metric? Like are we “cheating” the tokens/sec?

[12:33] Nina Petrova: No cheating. The metric measures produced tokens. If caching makes you faster, that’s real throughput. But we need to be consistent: the commitment would assume caching is enabled and you’re using the same prompt style.

[12:47] Miguel Santos: Does Redwood guarantee a tokens/sec number? Or a floor?

[12:52] Markus Klein: Today, Dedicated contracts are more about capacity and performance targets; we’re in the process of formalizing a throughput floor SLO. Practically, for a given shape and model, we’ll define a committed throughput floor under normal conditions.

[13:07] Markus Klein: “Normal” means: within max context, model pinned, no customer throttling or self-inflicted retry storms, and the deployment is warmed.

[13:18] Jason Wu: What’s “warmed” in time terms?

[13:20] Irene Choi: Usually a few minutes after deployment start or after a scale event. If you have a warm pool, it’s basically immediate. On Dedicated, we can maintain warm spares depending on tier, but that’s part of the packaging.

[13:35] Miguel Santos: We probably want warm spares because we can’t have cold starts at peak.

[13:39] Simran Kaur: That’s typically a higher tier or an add-on, but yes, for 2k QPS, cold start is not acceptable.

[13:48] Priya Desai: Sorry, what’s the difference between burst and warm spare? I keep mixing them.

[13:54] Markus Klein: Burst is: extra capacity beyond your committed floor for short periods. Warm spare is: pre-provisioned capacity that can take traffic immediately if a node dies or if you scale.

[14:10] Jason Wu: So the benchmark is on the committed pool, not burst.

[14:13] Simran Kaur: Correct. We benchmark the base pool. We can separately measure burst behavior but we don’t want to rely on burst as your steady state.

[14:24] Miguel Santos: If we start with A100 for cost reasons, is it straightforward to migrate to H100 later?

[14:30] Irene Choi: Operationally, yes. Same API, same config surface. But performance will change, so we re-baseline. We also need to check model compatibility with the kernel set.

[14:43] Nina Petrova: And memory differences can matter. If you’re right on the edge with context length on A100, H100 might allow more headroom.

[14:53] Priya Desai: What about L40S? It’s cheaper, right?

[14:56] Simran Kaur: It’s cheaper, but you trade off throughput and sometimes max context. It can be good for embeddings or lighter generation, but for high-QPS chat, we usually steer to A100/H100 for predictable TTFT.

[15:12] Jason Wu: Okay. We’re also curious about how you handle queueing. Like, do you have admission control?

[15:18] Nina Petrova: Yes. We cap queue depth and we have overload protection. Under saturation, we’d rather fail fast than let latency run away. For Dedicated, we set those thresholds to protect your throughput floor and tail latency.

[15:35] Miguel Santos: But if you fail fast, that hurts our app.

[15:38] Markus Klein: True, but it’s better to return a 429 quickly than to have everything hang for 20 seconds. Also, with Dedicated, if you’re saturating, the right fix is to increase committed capacity or split long-context traffic.

[15:55] Priya Desai: How do you recommend we split? By route? By model?

[15:59] Simran Kaur: Usually by route. “/chat” short context and “/chat-long” or “/summarize-transcript” with a separate concurrency cap or a separate pool.

[16:12] Jason Wu: We could do that. But we’d like one model if possible.

[16:16] Nina Petrova: You can keep one model and still split by route for scheduling reasons.

[16:22] Evan Brooks: Can you share benchmark methodology doc? We need to explain it internally.

[16:26] Simran Kaur: Yes, I’ll send a template and a short methodology write-up. It’s not super formal, but it covers the knobs and what we hold constant.

[16:37] Markus Klein: Let’s talk about what you need for a first pass sizing. Priya, can you send the histogram you mentioned? Hourly QPS and token percentiles.

[16:47] Priya Desai: Yep, we can do that.

[16:49] Jason Wu: We also have a sample of 1,000 prompts and expected outputs.

[16:53] Simran Kaur: Perfect. If you can sanitize and share those, we can run a replay-style benchmark.

[17:01] Miguel Santos: Data retention question: if we send prompts, do you store them?

[17:06] Markus Klein: For benchmarking, we can run in a secure bucket with limited access and delete after. We can also have you provide synthetic prompts that match length distribution without content.

[17:18] Jason Wu: Synthetic is fine. Length distribution matters more.

[17:21] Nina Petrova: Agreed. The main thing is tokenization behavior, but for most English text it’s close.

[17:29] Priya Desai: Back to streaming. How do you measure TTFT? We’ve seen providers count first chunk differently.

[17:35] Nina Petrova: We measure from request received at the inference gateway to the time we emit the first token from the model. So it includes queueing and prefill compute. It does not include client network. If you want end-to-end, we can help you measure with your client.

[17:55] Jason Wu: So if our clients are in Europe but the pool is in us-east, TTFT will look worse.

[17:59] Markus Klein: Exactly. For EU users you’ll likely want an EU region pool.

[18:04] Miguel Santos: We’ll get there, but step one is us-east.

[18:08] Irene Choi: For us-east, supply-wise, H100 is available but lead times can vary. A100 is more stable. If you need something in <30 days, A100 might be the safer bet.

[18:22] Miguel Santos: That’s good to know. We’re trying to launch a new feature end of April.

[18:27] Markus Klein: Timeline wise, we can do a benchmark this week, propose shape, and then talk commercial. Provisioning depends on tier/shape.

[18:37] Priya Desai: If you can, we’d love a number like “this shape supports X QPS at Y tokens.”

[18:43] Simran Kaur: We can give you that after we run your distribution. Without it, we can only give broad ranges.

[18:50] Jason Wu: OK.

[18:52] Markus Klein: Nina, can you explain one more nuance: prompt vs decode throughput. That’s where people get tripped up.

[18:59] Nina Petrova: Yes. There are two phases: prefill (processing input prompt tokens) and decode (generating output tokens). Many “tokens/sec” numbers you see are decode-focused. But long context increases prefill time a lot.

[19:15] Nina Petrova: In a mixed workload, a small percentage of long prompts can consume disproportionate GPU time. That’s why isolation or caps matter.

[19:26] Evan Brooks: So if we cap max context at 8k, does that make the pool stable?

[19:31] Nina Petrova: It helps. But even 8k prompts are heavy. Better is: cap + separate concurrency limit for long requests.

[19:41] Jason Wu: Does Redwood support “priority” scheduling? Like premium users vs free.

[19:46] Markus Klein: For Dedicated, yes, via tier-aware routing and admission controls. Within your deployment, we can implement priority queues at the gateway. It’s an enterprise feature—let’s scope it later.

[20:02] Miguel Santos: Not required for now.

[20:05] Simran Kaur: Another point: quantization. If you’re open to certain quant profiles, you can get more throughput. But it can affect quality.

[20:15] Priya Desai: We’re cautious. We can do evals, but we can’t degrade too much.

[20:21] Simran Kaur: Understood. In the benchmark plan we can test FP16 vs a safe quant config and compare.

[20:31] Jason Wu: Benchmarks you run, are they with continuous batching on? Some providers show numbers with it off.

[20:36] Nina Petrova: We run with our production batching configuration on. Otherwise it’s not representative. We can also show “batch off” to demonstrate the delta.

[20:48] Miguel Santos: And is caching on by default?

[20:51] Nina Petrova: Prefix caching is typically on when it’s beneficial. We’ll confirm it’s working with your prompt format.

[20:59] Markus Klein: Let’s shift to a proposed starting point. Based on what we heard: high QPS, streaming, p95 TTFT under 700ms, mostly short prompts, small long tail.

[21:12] Markus Klein: My gut says: start with an 8x H100 pool if timeline and budget allow, otherwise 8x A100 with strict caps on long-context concurrency.

[21:24] Jason Wu: We need a cost model. If H100 is 2x cost, we need to justify it.

[21:30] Irene Choi: H100 is higher cost but higher throughput, so cost per token can be better, depending on utilization. A100 might be fine if you’re not bottlenecked.

[21:42] Miguel Santos: We’ll need to see the benchmark.

[21:45] Markus Klein: Yep. That’s the right approach.

[21:48] Priya Desai: One more question: if you’re measuring tokens/sec, how do you handle internal retries, like if a GPU errors and you re-run?

[21:56] Nina Petrova: Great question. Internal retries would show up as increased latency and lower effective throughput. We also have separate error metrics. For SLO, we’re looking at delivered tokens/sec; internal failures reduce it.

[22:12] Jason Wu: So a hardware issue would count against the SLO.

[22:15] Markus Klein: Correct, if it impacts your floor in the measurement window, that’s on us.

[22:22] Miguel Santos: Speaking of windows, what window do you use? 1 minute? 1 hour?

[22:27] Nina Petrova: For reporting we look at rolling windows. Practically, we’ll evaluate over a window long enough to smooth noise but short enough to catch real issues—think minutes, not hours. The official SLO policy is being finalized.

[22:44] Jason Wu: Okay.

[22:46] Simran Kaur: For your internal planning, focus on steady-state sustained throughput, not a single-minute spike.

[22:54] Evan Brooks: If we do a deploy in us-east, can we later add eu-west and split traffic?

[23:00] Markus Klein: Yes. Same config layer. You’d typically have two Dedicated deployments and route by user region.

[23:09] Miguel Santos: Cool.

[23:11] Markus Klein: I think we should spend the remainder nailing the benchmark inputs so we can move quickly.

[23:18] Simran Kaur: I’ll send a template. But quick: we need three things.
1) Traffic curve (QPS by minute or by 5-min buckets) for peak day.
2) Token distributions: input/output percentiles and the fraction of long-context.
3) Any constraints: model candidates, max context you want, and whether function calling / JSON schema is required.

[23:45] Priya Desai: We don’t do tool calling right now. Mostly plain chat.

[23:49] Jason Wu: We do have a structured output mode for some routes, like JSON for metadata.

[23:54] Nina Petrova: That can impact decoding because of constrained sampling. But we can include it as a separate route. Don’t mix it with the main chat benchmark.

[24:06] Jason Wu: Okay.

[24:07] Miguel Santos: We also have a safety filter stage today. Not sure if that matters.

[24:12] Markus Klein: If it’s outside the model (like a separate classifier), it doesn’t affect the inference pool, but it affects your end-to-end. For this benchmark, we focus on the model serving.

[24:25] Evan Brooks: What about multi-tenancy? We have multiple products. Would that be separate routes or separate deployments?

[24:31] Simran Kaur: Depends on isolation requirements. In Dedicated you can do multiple routes in one deployment with per-route quotas. If you want strict isolation, separate deployments.

[24:44] Jason Wu: For now one deployment is fine.

[24:47] Markus Klein: Great.

[24:49] Priya Desai: Can we get access to the dashboards you mentioned? Like GPU utilization and queue time.

[24:55] Markus Klein: During a pilot, yes. For production, the Redwood Console shows those metrics and SLO status. We can also export to your Datadog if needed.

[25:08] Miguel Santos: We’re a Datadog shop.

[25:10] Nina Petrova: We have integrations. We can talk later.

[25:14] Markus Klein: Alright. I’m going to pause and see if you have any remaining questions about shapes.

[25:20] Jason Wu: One more: if we go 8x A100, do we have a path to add two more nodes? Like scale out.

[25:27] Irene Choi: We can scale out by adding more nodes, but it changes the communication pattern depending on the model. Many models run per node; scaling out is just more replicas. That’s the common pattern for high QPS: many replicas.

[25:42] Nina Petrova: Exactly. For high QPS, replication is your friend. Sharding is more for very large models.

[25:51] Priya Desai: So we might end up with, like, two 8x nodes eventually.

[25:55] Irene Choi: Potentially, yes, depending on required throughput.

[25:59] Markus Klein: That’s also why we want to understand your concurrency and duration. It’s not just QPS.

[26:06] Miguel Santos: Makes sense.

[26:09] Markus Klein: Okay, last section—recap and next steps.

[26:13] Markus Klein: Simran will send the benchmark template by Wednesday. Priya/Jason you’ll send histograms and traffic curves by end of week. Irene/Nina will propose 1–2 shapes in us-east with expected ranges. Then we’ll meet next week to review.

[26:31] Jason Wu: Works.

[26:33] Priya Desai: Yep.

[26:35] Miguel Santos: Thanks. This was helpful.

[26:38] Markus Klein: Great. We’ll follow up by email. End of call.
